cases.answer: SQLite has offered WAL mode since version 3.7.0. In WAL mode, writers and readers can run at the same time, although there can only be one writer at a time. A checkpoint runs automatically once the WAL file reaches 1000 pages, and the WAL file is normally named after the database file with a "-wal" suffix.

cases.answer: WAL works best with smaller transactions. For transactions larger than about 10 megabytes, the traditional rollback journal modes will likely be faster, and transactions in excess of a gigabyte may fail with an I/O or disk-full error. In applications that mostly read, WAL can be roughly 1% or 2% slower than rollback journaling. Write transactions are fast because the content only has to be written once.

cases.answer: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, but it must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader. As a result, a long-running read transaction can prevent the checkpointer from making progress. If there is always at least one active reader, checkpoints still complete, just more slowly. Running manual checkpoints with SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART guarantees that readers are never blocked. Checkpoint starvation is the most common cause of WAL file growth in production systems.

cases.answer: Unlike the other journaling modes, the WAL journal mode is persistent: if a process sets WAL mode, then closes and reopens the database, it comes back in WAL mode. This means applications can be converted to WAL without changing the application itself. WAL mode was first released in July 2010, and it is the default journal mode for databases created on Android. The WAL file should be kept with the database when the database is copied, and the safest way to remove a WAL file is to delete it manually after all processes have stopped.

cases.answer: WAL mode first appeared in SQLite 3.7.0. Because journal_mode=WAL is persistent, simply closing and reopening a WAL database is not enough to change its page size; you have to switch back to a rollback journal mode first. From version 3.7.0 until 3.22.0, reading a WAL-mode database required write access. SQLite's default page size is 4096 bytes. Converting a database to WAL fails if the VFS does not support the necessary shared-memory primitives, in which case the journal_mode pragma returns an error.

cases.answer: Redis offers three appendfsync policies. With appendfsync always, Redis calls fsync every time new commands are appended to the AOF, which is very safe but very slow. The default policy is appendfsync no, which leaves flushing to the operating system; on Linux this normally means data is flushed every 30 seconds. With everysec you may lose about one second of data in a disaster. Because fsync runs on a background thread, the main thread never has to wait for disk I/O, and appendfsync always typically cuts write throughput by more than half.

cases.answer: RDB is a very compact, single-file point-in-time representation of the dataset, which makes it well suited for backups. During an RDB save the parent process never performs disk I/O itself, because a forked child does all the work. RDB files are compressed with LZF by default. Since Redis 7.0.0 the AOF is split into a base file and incremental files, which are tracked by a manifest file. If the dataset is very big and the CPU is slow, fork() can make Redis stop serving clients for up to one second.

cases.answer: If you increment a counter 100 times, the AOF ends up with 100 entries even though only the final value matters, so 99 of them are not needed to rebuild the current state. To deal with this, BGREWRITEAOF writes the shortest sequence of commands needed to rebuild the current dataset in memory, and like RDB saving, the rewrite is done by a forked child process. Automatic log rewriting has been supported since Redis 2.2. The Redis documentation recommends running AOF alone for most deployments.
